title: An asymmetric photothermal platform for coupled seawater splitting and desalination

paper_content.abstract: Photocatalytic seawater splitting provides a sustainable route to green hydrogen, but faces barriers of inefficiency and scalability. Graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4, CN) offers saline tolerance, yet its catalytic potential requires atomic-level control of structure and charge dynamics. Herein, we design three single-atom Co configurations on CN, including symmetric Co–N4, vacancy-anchored Co–N3, and asymmetric Co–N4. The asymmetric Co–N4 in hierarchically porous carbon nitride (CoSA-hCN) introduces second-shell carbon vacancies that reshape electronic asymmetry and charge dynamics, establishing a robust pathway for effective salinity-mediated charge transfer and in situ Pt photodeposition for H2 evolution. On a scalable 60 cm2 floating photothermal platform under 1 sun, H2 production (47.7 mmol m−2 h−1) and interfacial seawater evaporation (1.88 kg m−2 h−1) are achieved directly from natural seawater. In this work, we offer design principles for a single-atom catalyst on scalable photothermal platform for coupled seawater splitting and desalination.
paper_content.introduction:
Recently, seawater splitting to hydrogen has been a research hot spot.1–4 Compared with electrocatalysis,4,5 solar seawater splitting will deliver green H2 at a global scale,1,2 while seawater’s ionic complexity heavily corrodes most catalysts (Supplementary Fig. 1a).6,7 Graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4, CN) showed somewhat tolerance to saline environments,8,9 where polar surface and ion-catalyst interactions may enhance charge separation and redox kinetics.10 Nevertheless, its intrinsic catalytic activity remains limited by poor charge transfer and insufficient active sites. Also, the underlying mechanisms governing these processes have been insufficiently explored, and unlocking the full catalytic potential of CN requires precise structural engineering that integrates active-site design with controlled electronic and geometric modulation.11,12 Recent advances highlight CN-supported single-atom metal photocatalysts (SACs) as an ideal platform,13–15 yet their translation to seawater splitting has scarcely been realized, where complex ionic matrices demand in-depth mechanistic understanding and design strategies. In CN-integrated SACs, first-shell vacancy engineering and coordination number modulation of metal centers has been widely studied.16,17 By contrast, second-shell asymmetry, arising from nearby vacancies or ligand field distortions, has been recognized to strongly tune orbital hybridization and charge redistribution in carbon-supported single-atom electrocatalysts,18,19 however, its role in CN-SACs, particularly in shaping photocatalysis and ionic interactions in seawater conditions, has rarely been explored. Advancing understandings of coordination asymmetry at different atomic levels will be essential for guiding next-generation CN-SAC designs for solar H2 production from seawater.

Beyond atomic-level photocatalyst engineering, integration of materials into scalable and robust systems is equally important for advancing practical seawater splitting. Direct seawater utilization can significantly enhance sustainability by reducing freshwater dependence in arid and coastal regions.20 A unified platform that simultaneously produces H2 and freshwater would unlock the full potential of seawater, offering a broadly applicable strategy for sustainable energy and water supply.20,21 Yet, the inherently distinct physicochemical demands of photocatalysis and desalination have led to their separate treatment in previous investigations.22–24 Integration attempts, such as sheet-assisted architectures20 or photothermal evaporative substrates,25 remain largely a proof-of-concept. These systems often suffer from structural complexity, limited scalability, and trade-offs between freshwater and hydrogen yields. These limitations highlight the need for a structurally simple and scalable platform that can simultaneously deliver efficient photocatalysis and desalination.

In this work, we establish a molecular-level coordination-engineering strategy to construct three single-atom Co configurations on CN: symmetric Co–N4 (CoSA-CN), vacancy-anchored Co–N3 (CoSA@hCN), and asymmetric Co–N4 with second-shell carbon vacancies (CoSA-hCN). The asymmetric coordination in CoSA-hCN induces a distinct electronic-asymmetry and facilitates electron transfer from Co to the CN framework for efficient in situ Pt cocatalyst photodeposition. From a catalyst design perspective, this tailored coordination and surface charge strongly promote selective interactions with seawater ions and improve salinity-mediated charge transfer (Supplementary Fig. 1b). Under visible light irradiation, CoSA-hCN exhibits 4- and 3-fold higher H2 evolution rate than CoSA-CN and CoSA@hCN, respectively. Remarkably, CoSA-hCN presents a distinct solar-induced photothermal effect, contributing to its record-high performance. Most importantly, we integrate CoSA-hCN into a floating photothermal platform using a 60 cm2 commercial sponge support (Fig. 1a) to couple efficient H2 generation with seawater desalination (Supplementary Fig. 1b). This work demonstrates that asymmetric single-atom site design can be easily translated into device-level integration and the sponge-supported floating architecture provides a structurally simple and modular basis for real seawater operation. These advances in atomic-level innovation and scalability design establish a general blueprint for future solar energy conversion and clean water technologies.
paper_content.results:
Catalyst synthesis and characterizations

All CN-SACs were synthesized via pyrolysis of dicyandiamide (DCDA) and cobalt (II) acetylacetonate (Co(acac)2) precursors (Fig. 1b-d). Direct pyrolysis led to immobilization of Co single-atoms (CoSA) within melon polymer chains, producing CoSA-CN with a compact, non-porous morphology (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 2-4). To construct hierarchical porous SACs with an enlarged surface area (Supplementary Fig. 3-5 and Supplementary Table 1), we adopted a silica template-assisted pyrolysis strategy. Close-packed silica spheres provide a confinement effect to promote single-atom loading.13,14,26 Additionally, silica templating introduces structural modifications such as vacancy formation,27,28 yet its influences on the coordination environment of single-atom centers remain unexplored. Accordingly, a one-step silica template-assisted pyrolysis method was used to induce vacancy formation and modulate the local electronic structure, thereby breaking the coordination symmetry of Co centers and producing CoSA-hCN (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 6). For comparison, Co atoms were anchored onto pre-formed hCN via a multi-step self-assembly and pyrolysis method to produce CoSA@hCN catalysts (Fig. 1d). All samples show similar Co loadings, as determined by inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES, Supplementary Fig. 7).

Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark field scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC HAADF-STEM, Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. 8) and energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX, Fig. 1f) mapping images confirm atomically dispersed Co across all catalysts. This aligns with X-ray diffraction (XRD), showing no detectable Co-related crystalline peak (Supplementary Fig. 9). CoSA@hCN and CoSA-hCN show weakened (100) and (002) peaks, suggesting NH3-induced C atom etching and reduced stacking periodicity.28,29 X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) reveals a notable decrease in the atomic C/N ratio in CoSA-hCN and CoSA@hCN than CoSA-CN, confirming the formation of C vacancies (Supplementary Fig. 10). Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra show intensified −OH/−NH/−NH2 stretching at 2800-3600 cm−1 (Supplementary Fig. 11), further confirming C atom removal and amine group formation.30 Solid-state 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy was conducted to pinpoint vacancy locations (Fig. 1g). The declining i1:i2 ratio (characteristic C atoms in N=C–N to N=C–N(NH2) from CoSA-CN to CoSA-hCN and CoSA@hCN) evidences the loss of C atoms in the N=C–Nx motif. Solid-state electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy shows that CoSA-hCN exhibits the strongest signal at the g-value of 2.004, indicating the most abundant unpaired π-electrons localized at the C vacancy sites (Supplementary Fig. 12). In contrast, CoSA@hCN shows a slightly weaker signal than hCN, implying partial vacancy occupation by Co atoms in CoSA@hCN.31

Synchrotron-based X-ray absorption spectroscopy was used to investigate the structural and electronic properties of catalysts. The C K-edge X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES, Supplementary Fig. 13a) spectra show a weakened π*(C−N−C) peak in CoSA-hCN, indicating disruption of the C−N−C coordination,15 likely caused by the disorder in the sp2 in-plane structure by C vacancies. This may induce interlayer C–N interaction and create conductive paths across the layers for improved charge transfer.32 N K-edge XANES spectra reveal attenuated π* resonances for triangular edge π*(C–N–C) and bridging N (π*(N–C)) in CoSA-hCN than hCN33 (Supplementary Fig. 13b). This suggests orbital hybridization and electron donation from Co to N atoms, considering lower electronegativity of Co relative to C and N.32 Meanwhile, Co K-edge XANES (Fig. 1h) reveals a positive shift in CoSA-hCN, indicating increased electropositivity and charge delocalization.34,35 The weaker pre-edge peak and stronger white-line peak in CoSA-hCN suggest the reduced symmetry and rearranged charge polarization.34,36

Fourier-transformed Co K-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra (Fig. 1i) show a main peak at ~1.6 Å at R space for all samples, corresponding to Co–N first-shell coordination. CoSA@hCN exhibits reduced peak intensity, indicating a lower first-shell coordination number than CoSA-CN and CoSA-hCN. EXAFS fitting results reveal that the first-shell coordination numbers of CoSA-CN, CoSA-hCN and CoSA@hCN are 4.3, 4.4, and 3.3. respectively (Supplementary Fig. 14 and Supplementary Table 2). The Co–C second-shell coordination (~2.5 Å, referenced against CoPc) shows diminished intensity in CoSA-hCN relative to CoSA-CN, reflecting C vacancies-induced loss of second-shell C atoms. For CoSA@hCN, the weakened second-shell Co–C signal and broadened first-shell peak suggest that Co atoms are anchored at vacancy sites, where shortened Co–C distances lead to overlapping Co–N/C scattering paths in the first-shell region. The absence of Co–Co (2.2 Å) coordination confirms single-atom feature of all samples. Wavelet transform (WT) analysis further validates exclusive Co–N coordination without Co–Co or Co–O contributions (Fig. 1j). Collectively, the above structural characterizations reveal symmetric Co–N4 configurations for CoSA-CN, Co–N3 at C vacancies for CoSA@hCN and asymmetric Co–N4 with second-shell C vacancy for CoSA-hCN, enabling distinct electronic modulation.

Structure-property correlation

To elucidate the impact of asymmetric coordination on electronic modulation, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Local structural models of CoSA-CN, CoSA-hCN, and CoSA@hCN were constructed and optimized to explore how coordination symmetry affects electronic structure and charge transport (Supplementary Fig. 15, Supplementary Data 1). The spatial charge density distribution in Fig. 2a and Supplementary Fig. 15 shows that introducing the C vacancy in CoSA-hCN induces charge redistribution, with electron accumulation on the tri-s-triazine framework. Bader charge analysis reveals that the amount of electrons transferred from Co to surrounding N atoms increases from 0.90 (CoSA-CN) to 1.12 (CoSA@hCN) and 1.13 e (CoSA-hCN). The total and projected density of states (DOS) further highlight these differences (Fig. 2b). In CoSA-hCN, the Co-d states show an enrichment and broadening near the Fermi level (EF), as well as significant Co–N hybridization. The increased near-EF Co-d spectral weight provides more accessible states for charge transfer. Interestingly, the projected DOS appears symmetric in CoSA-CN and CoSA@hCN, suggesting weak hybridization,37 while CoSA-hCN displays an irregular and asymmetric line shape, reflecting stronger orbital hybridization, which facilitates charge delocalization and charge transfer. The spin density plot (Supplementary Fig. 16) further reveals localized spin polarization on the Co atom and neighboring N sites. This confirms that the asymmetric coordination environment induces a localized unpaired electron distribution, which may facilitate spin-selective charge transfer and thereby enhance the photocatalytic activity of CoSA-hCN.

We further examined the influences of structural variations on electronic properties and carrier dynamics. Steady-state photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy in Fig. 2c shows that the emission intensities follow: CN > hCN > CoSA-CN > CoSA@hCN > CoSA-hCN, implying the maximally inhibited intrinsic radiative recombination of photocarriers in CoSA-hCN. A slight red shift of the emission peak from 466 (CoSA-CN) to 468 (CoSA@hCN) and 470 nm (CoSA-hCN) is attributed to the increased trap state and defect density (Supplementary Fig. 17). Time-resolved PL (TRPL) spectroscopy reveals a decreased average fluorescence lifetime (τave) from 5.24 (CoSA-CN) to 5.05 (CoSA@hCN) and 3.83 ns for CoSA-hCN, suggesting accelerated charge transfer in CoSA-hCN (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Table 3). The shortened lifetime indicates an increased contribution of non-radiative recombination pathways. Such non-radiative relaxation is expected to contribute to localized photothermal heating under illumination,38 which may support faster interfacial reaction kinetics. The findings of electronic function align well with the DFT simulations, confirming that the vacancy-induced symmetry breaking could facilitate more charge delocalization and promote carrier dynamics. These calculations are based on idealized models and do not capture the full surface complexity or dynamic ionic environment under operating conditions; therefore, they provide qualitative rather than quantitative insight into structure-property relationships.

Solid-state EPR was performed to track light-induced electron delocalization within the vacancy-engineered framework (Fig. 2e). Upon light irradiation, CoSA-hCN exhibits a pronounced intensity increase, indicating enhanced delocalization of photocarriers across the π-conjugated network. This is attributed to the electronic perturbation introduced by carbon vacancies. In further assessing charge transport capability, electrochemical impedance spectra profiles indicate that CoSA-hCN exhibits the lowest charge transfer resistance among all catalysts (Supplementary Fig. 18). Consistently, CoSA-hCN shows the highest photocurrent density, confirming its great capability for charge separation and migration (Supplementary Fig. 19). The electronic band structures were evaluated using UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS, Supplementary Fig. 20) and valence band (VB) XPS to determine valence band maximum differences (Supplementary Fig. 21) as well as ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) to extract the absolute valence band position (Supplementary Fig. 22). These measurements show that CoSA-hCN possesses the most negative conduction band potential, favoring 2H+/H2 photoreduction (Supplementary Fig. 23).

In photocatalytic H2 evolution systems by CN-SACs, Pt nanoparticles were typically introduced via in situ photodeposition using H2PtCl6.39–43 Their formation is inherently a charge transfer-driven process and highly sensitive to the photocatalyst’s electronic structure. However, the underlying mechanisms governing Pt deposition and its interaction with single-atom sites remain insufficiently understood. Building on the above insights into asymmetric coordination and electronic modulation, we further explored how local coordination features affect cocatalyst integration and interfacial charge transfer dynamics. To probe the dynamics of in situ Pt photodeposition on SACs, we conducted open-circuit potential (OCP) measurements (Fig. 2f). Under light irradiation, all catalysts exhibited gradual photoanodic shifts, indicating the electron extraction. Notably, CoSA-hCN showed a greater potential increase upon H2PtCl6 addition than others, suggesting more efficient electron transfer from the photoexcited matrix to reduce Pt4+ and facilitate Pt nanoparticle formation. The presence of Pt nanoparticles was verified in HAADF-STEM and EDX mappings (Supplementary Fig. 24 and inset in Fig. 2f). ICP-OES analysis indicates comparable Pt loadings across the three catalysts, with CoSA-hCN exhibiting the highest Pt loading at 4.08 wt% (Supplementary Fig. 25a). This indicates more favorable Pt photodeposition on CoSA-hCN. TEM images show that the Pt nanoparticles on CoSA-hCN and CoSA@hCN are more evenly dispersed and exhibit a narrower size distribution, typically below 5 nm, whereas Pt on CoSA-CN presents less uniform dispersion and shows larger aggregates (Supplementary Fig. 25b-d), reflecting the distinct structural and electronic characteristics of the supports.

To probe the oxidation states and interfacial electronic interactions of photodeposited Pt species, we performed XPS analysis of samples before and after deposition. Upon Pt loading, N 1s peaks of CoSA-hCN slightly shifted to higher binding energies (Supplementary Fig. 26), suggesting electron transfer from the substrate to Pt. In contrast, negligible spectral changes were observed in hCN and CoSA-CN; minor in CoSA@hCN (Supplementary Fig. 27-29), indicating relatively weak Pt-substrate interaction and less effective Pt anchoring. The Pt 4f spectra of CoSA-hCN after photodeposition display distinct peaks at 73.0 and 76.3 eV for Pt2+ species from partial reduction of H2PtCl6, along with sub-peaks at 70.8 and 74.6 eV for metallic Pt0 (Fig. 2g). The coexistence of Pt0 and Pt2+ species implies a dual functional role, where Pt0 facilitates proton reduction and Pt2+ prevents the undesirable H2 backward reaction.44 Other samples exhibited weak or indistinct Pt 4f signals under identical photodeposition conditions. These differences highlight the favorable electronic structure of CoSA-hCN for Pt4+ photoreduction and dual-functional Pt generation, ultimately enhancing H2 photoproduction. To further study the electronic interaction, we performed theoretical calculations on the optimized Pt-loaded CoSA-CN, CoSA-hCN and CoSA@hCN models (Supplementary Data 2). DOS profiles in Supplementary Fig. 30 reveal that CoSA-hCN induces a more pronounced redistribution of electronic states near the Fermi level, indicating stronger electronic coupling between Pt and the Co single-atom center. Bader charge analysis (Supplementary Fig. 31) shows that Pt undergoes pronounced electron enrichment upon interacting with the substrates, confirming spontaneous interfacial charge transfer consistent with its role as an efficient electron acceptor for proton reduction. Among all configurations, Pt on Co-hCN exhibits the most negative Bader charge, further confirming the strongest electronic interaction.

The charge transfer on Co sites was also investigated. Post-deposition Co K-edge XANES spectra were re-examined in pure water containing H2PtCl6 under visible light irradiation. All catalysts display a slight edge shift toward higher energy, consistent with electron transfer from Co centers to reduce Pt4+ during Pt nucleation (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Fig. 32). With the addition of TEOA after reaction, CoSA-hCN shows a small shift toward lower energy, reflecting the reductive action of TEOA on the Co sites (Fig. 2h). Fourier-transformed Co K-edge EXAFS analysis indicates the Co active sites still preserve their singly dispersed nature after operation (Supplementary Fig. 33). The enhanced white line intensity suggests reduced local symmetry and increased unoccupied 3d states around the Co centers. TRPL spectroscopy highlights the dominant role of single-atom Co in facilitating charge transport, with minimal contribution from Pt (Supplementary Fig. 34-35). These findings support a directional charge transfer mechanism: photoexcited electrons first transiently stabilize at the redox-flexible Co sites, then relay through surrounding N sites, and ultimately reach Pt cocatalysts to drive proton reduction (Fig. 2i).

Photocatalytic H2 production from seawater

Photocatalytic H2 evolution performances were evaluated under visible light irradiation using TEOA as a sacrificial agent and in situ photodeposited Pt as the cocatalyst (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 36). Among all catalysts, CoSA-hCN exhibited the highest H2 production rate of 6.4 ± 0.2 mmol g–1 h–1 in artificial seawater (ASTM D1141-98 (2013) standard, Supplementary Table 4), which is 4- and 3-fold higher than that of CoSA-CN and CoSA@hCN, respectively. As discussed above, this enhanced activity primarily arises from the asymmetric Co–N4 coordination and vacancy-induced electronic modulation, which strengthen charge separation and promote efficient in situ Pt photodeposition, while physicochemical improvements such as higher surface area provide additional contributions. The apparent quantum efficiency (AQE) reached 8.96% at 420 nm. Under combined UV and visible light irradiation, the H2 evolution rate of CoSA-hCN increased to 8.2 ± 0.3 mmol g–1 h–1 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 36b). When operated without temperature control, photothermal self-heating raised the system temperature to ~65 °C (Supplementary Fig. 37), boosting the rate to 22.5 ± 1.2 mmol g–1 h–1, 2.7-fold increase compared to that at 25 °C. This photothermal enhancement effect, evidenced by the experimentally observed temperature increase of the reaction system, has rarely been reported in CN-SAC and CN-based systems for photocatalytic H2 production from water or seawater. It enables an competitive H2 evolution activity with previously reported CN-SAC photocatalysts (primarily evaluated in water)39–43,45–50, and CN-based photocatalysts in seawater8,51–59 (Supplementary Table 5). The structural stability of CoSA-hCN was verified by cyclic tests and unchanged XRD pattern, FTIR spectrum and C/N K-edge XANES of the post-reaction samples (Supplementary Fig. 38). Notably, CoSA-hCN demonstrates proof-of-concept photocatalytic performance in natural seawater under laboratory conditions, achieving a H2 production rate of 5.9 mmol g–1 h–1 in natural seawater (Fig. 3a). Furthermore, photoelectrochemical corrosion tests (Fig. 3c) revealed that CoSA-hCN exhibits a lower corrosion potential (0.56 V) than CN (0.62 mV), hCN (0.69 V), CoSA-CN (0.60 V), and CoSA@hCN (0.58 V) under simulated sunlight irradiation. This suggests the robust anti-corrosion capability of CoSA-hCN, highlighting its potential for real-life applications in marine environments.

To explore how interfacial characteristics of catalysts correlate with their behaviors in seawater, we studied the interfacial wettability and surface charge properties. As shown in Fig. 3d, the contact angle of CoSA-hCN decreased from 59.7° in pure water to 47.9° in seawater, indicating enhanced hydrophilicity under saline conditions. Compared with CoSA@hCN (64.6°) and CoSA-CN (56.1°), the enhanced hydrophilicity in CoSA-hCN promotes better contact between the catalyst surface and seawater matrix, facilitating mass transfer and interfacial reactivity (Supplementary Fig. 39). Zeta potential measurements revealed that CoSA-hCN possessed a more negatively charged surface than CoSA@hCN and CoSA-CN (Fig. 3e). This may help suppress local Cl− accumulation at the interface for undesired side reactions. Meanwhile, the negatively charged surface electrostatically attracts seawater cations (e.g., Na+, Mg2+, Ca2+), which may modulate surface polarization and interfacial charge distribution, thereby enhancing electron mobility.1 Simultaneously, H⁺ ions are drawn toward the negatively charged surface, promoting H+-coupled electron transfer for H2 evolution. Theoretically, Gibbs free energy calculations confirm that CoSA-hCN exhibits the great intrinsic activity for proton adsorption and H2 evolution (Supplementary Fig. 40, the atomic coordinates of the computational models have been provided in Supplementary Data 3). Simplified computational models are employed to evaluate intrinsic proton adsorption, while the effects of cocatalysts and ionic species under realistic reaction conditions are not explicitly included.

To clarify the influence of specific seawater ions on H2 production, we evaluated individual salts. As shown in Fig. 3a, NaCl led to the highest H2 evolution rate, outperforming MgCl2 and CaCl2. TRPL spectroscopy was used to investigate the effect of different saline components on charge transfer (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 41-43). Fig. 3g shows that NaCl exhibits the most pronounced effect in shortening carrier lifetimes, reflecting its dominant role in promoting charge transfer. Given NaCl’s important effect, DFT calculations were performed to evaluate the adsorption behavior of Na+ and Cl− on different catalysts (Supplementary Data 4). As revealed by the adsorption energy (Eads), CoSA-CN and CoSA@hCN possess more negative Eads of Cl− than Na+, indicating higher affinity to Cl− (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Fig. 44). In comparison, CoSA-hCN can significantly enhance the adsorption of Na+ (Eads of −3.21 eV), showing a preference to Na+ than Cl− (−3.19 eV). Relative adsorption energies (Fig. 3h, Supplementary Fig. 45 and Supplementary Data 5) further suggest that the asymmetric atomic structure of CoSA-hCN promotes selective adsorption of seawater cations over Cl⁻, favoring cation interaction (Fig. 3i). This selectivity suppresses chlorine by-product formation, improving anticorrosion ability,60 while the cation adsorption induces strong polarization and facilitates photocarrier transport.1 Furthermore, band center analysis (Supplementary Fig. 46) shows that CoSA-hCN exhibits optimal orbital alignment for efficient reactant sorption and favorable reaction kinetics. Taken together, asymmetric electronic structure engineering of CoSA-hCN enables selective ion interactions and salinity-mediated charge transfer, thereby enhancing photocatalytic H2 production in saline environments.

Scaled-up seawater splitting and desalination under practical conditions

To evaluate device-level feasibility, we developed a pilot-scale photothermal device to simultaneously achieve H2 evolution and seawater desalination (Fig. 4a-b and Supplementary Fig. 47). A floatable sponge photoreactor was constructed using a commercial sponge (L100 × W60 × H50 mm), featuring a white melamine‐formaldehyde (MF) foam at the upper layer and a black synthetic fiber at lower layer (Supplementary Fig. 48). Photocatalysts were immobilized onto the upper layer via a simple dip-coating method (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 49-50). The melamine foam contains abundant N–H and C–H functional groups that provide favorable sites for anchoring CoSA-hCN during impregnation (Supplementary Fig. 51). A mechanical stability test demonstrated the robust interfacial bonding between the photocatalyst and the melamine support (Supplementary Fig. 52). During operation, capillary action transports seawater from the base to the catalyst-coated surface (Fig. 4b-c), while the open-cell MF provides strong buoyancy to keep the catalytic surface afloat (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 53). The hydrophobic backing further enhances flotation by trapping air within its porous matrix and distributing flotation across the photoreactor, preventing waterlogging and ensuring full light exposure of the catalyst surface. This structure facilitates a unidirectional seawater flow, improving reactant delivery and promoting H2 evolution. Simultaneously, photothermal heating evaporates seawater at the interface, and the resulting vapor condenses on the overhead cover and is collected as freshwater, enabling integrated H2 and freshwater co-production.

Under simulated sun irradiation (average 103 mW cm–2) and ambient conditions (~25 °C, ~40% humidity), the Pt-deposited CoSA-hCN-embedded sponge exhibited rapid surface heating to 37.5 °C within 10 min and stabilized at ~45 °C (Fig. 4e and Supplementary Fig. 54), significantly higher than the bulk sponge (~33 °C, Supplementary Fig. 55). This photothermal enhancement enabled a higher evaporation rate of 1.75 kg m−2 h−1 from artificial seawater (Fig. 4f), outperforming the bulk sponge (1.05 kg m−2 h−1). The evaporation rate reached 1.88 kg m−2 h−1 in 6 h from natural seawater (Supplementary Fig. 56). To assess the desalination performance, we quantified the amount of freshwater condensed during a 6 h light-irradiation run in the coupled H2 evolution and desalination process (Fig. 4g-h). The freshwater yield at 7.5 kg m−2, with ion concentrations (Na+, Mg2+, Ca2+ and K+) in the condensate reduced below the World Health Organization drinking threshold (Fig. 4i and Supplementary Fig. 57). The system also demonstrates good applicability with natural seawater, yielding 8.3 kg m−2 purified water.

Simultaneous photocatalytic H2 production was realized using Pt-deposited CoSA-hCN-immobilized sponge (Fig. 5a-b), achieving a H2 production rate of 55.3 ± 4.1 mmol m−2 h−1 in artificial seawater under 6 h light irradiation (Fig. 5c-d and Supplementary Fig. 58), and maintaining high efficiency under realistic aqueous solutions (Supplementary Fig. 59). Triethanolamine functioned both as a stabilizer for catalyst immobilization and as a sacrificial electron donor (Fig. 5c). We further validated the generality of the integrated system by replacing catalysts with commercial TiO2 (P25). Under identical conditions, P25 showed a relatively lower H2 production rate (Supplementary Fig. 60), confirming that the enhanced performance in our system arises from the synergistic coupling between CoSA-hCN and the photothermal reactor. The system exhibited stable long-term performance for H2 production and seawater desalination (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 61-62), with minimal catalyst leaching (Supplementary Fig. 63). The unchanged C and N K-edge profiles indicate that the CoSA-hCN catalysts remain structurally stable after the operation (Supplementary Fig. 64). During cycling tests, catalyst retention at the sponge surface was maintained via gravity-assisted redistribution. This concept can be adapted for large-scale floating systems by incorporating passive tilting or slow rotational movement, allowing the catalyst layer to self-redistribute under operational conditions in open-water environments. Compared to state-of-the-art floatable photocatalytic systems20,21,25,61,62 (Supplementary Table 6), our platform features simple and modular design that allows facile fabrication through a one-step dipping process. It provides a practically viable strategy to integrate efficient hydrogen production and seawater purification.
paper_content.methods:
Materials

All chemicals used are of an analytical grade without further purification. Ammonium hydroxide solution (NH3·H2O, 28.0 - 30.0% NH3 basis), ammonium hydrogen difluoride (NH4HF2, pure), acetone (≥99.5%), cobalt(II) acetylacetonate (Co(C5H7O2)2, ≥99.0%), dicyandiamide (DCDA, 99%), ethanol (≥99.9%, absolute, analytical level), isopropyl alcohol (≥99.9%), and tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS, ≥99.0%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ cm−1) was used. Artificial seawater was prepared using the ASTM D1141-98(2021) standard, specifically, 24.53 g L–1 NaCl, 5.20 g L–1 MgCl2, 4.09 g L–1 Na2SO4, 1.16 g L–1 CaCl2, 0.69 g L–1 KCl, and 0.20 g L–1 NaHCO3 solution. Natural seawater was collected on the Grange Beach in Adelaide, South Australia. A commercial sponge (Big Job Magic Eraser, Chux) was purchased from a Woolworths supermarket in Adelaide, South Australia.

Fabrication of ordered silica templates

Ordered silica microsphere templates were synthesized using a modified Stöber method. In this process, Solution A was prepared by adding 192 mL of ethanol to 8 mL of TEOS and stirring at 500 rpm at 25 °C. Simultaneously, Solution B was made by combining 14 mL NH3·H2O, 56.6 mL ethanol, and 29.4 mL ultrapure water, also stirred at 500 rpm at 25 °C. After 30 min, Solution B was gradually and slowly added to Solution A while stirring at 750 rpm. The resulting mixture was centrifuged at 18,900 g using a high-speed constant temperature centrifuge at 20 °C. The collected silica was washed with ultrapure water to remove residuals, dried in a preheated oven at 60 °C overnight, and then ground and dispersed in 5 wt% ultrapure water. This solution was placed into vials and subjected to ultrasonication, followed by evaporation in a preheated oven at 110 °C for 24 h, allowing the silica microspheres to self-assemble into silica strips on the vial walls.

Fabrication of pristine carbon nitride (CN)

Pristine CN was synthesized by calcining 0.6 g of DCDA at 520 °C for 2 h (2 °C·min–1), followed by further calcination at 550 °C for an additional 2 h (4 °C·min–1) under an argon (Ar) atmosphere. The resulting CN solid was washed thoroughly with ultrapure water and subsequently dried at 60 °C.

Fabrication of hierarchical porous carbon nitride (hCN)

The hCN was synthesized by calcining DCDA with the help of a silica template. Specifically, 0.6 g DCDA was ground with 1 g silica template and subsequently calcined at 520 °C for 2 h (2 °C min–1), followed by further calcination at 550 °C for an additional 2 h (4 °C min–1) under an Ar atmosphere. The resulting product was etched with 50 mL of a 4 mol L–1 NH4HF2 solution (pH of 4.5 ± 0.3) for 48 h to remove the silica template. The as-obtained hCN solids were then washed several times with ultrapure water and dried overnight at 60 °C.

Fabrication of CoSA-hCN

A mixture of DCDA and Co(C5H7O2)2 was dissolved in a 300 mL solution comprising ethanol and acetone in a ratio of 1:1. The solution was stirred at 400 rpm and heated to 75 °C for 2 days for evaporation. The resulting solid was washed with ultrapure water several times and dried in a preheated oven at 60 °C overnight. The collected solids were ground. Subsequently, 0.6 g of collected solids were further ground with 1 g silica template, and calcined at 520 °C for 2 h (2 °C min–1), followed by 550 °C for 2 h (4 °C min–1) in Ar. The product was etched with 50 mL of 4 M NH4HF2 solution (pH of 4.5 ± 0.3) for 48 h to remove the silica template. Finally, the CoSA-hCN solid was collected, rinsed with ultrapure water, and dried overnight at 60 °C.

Fabrication of CoSA-CN

A mixture of DCDA and Co(C5H7O2)2 was dissolved in a 300 mL solution comprising ethanol and acetone in a 1:1 ratio. The solution was stirred at 400 rpm and heated to 75 °C for 2 days for evaporation. The resulting solid was washed with ultrapure water several times and dried in a preheated oven at 60 °C overnight. The collected solids were ground and calcined at 520 °C for 2 h (2 °C min–1), followed by 550 °C for 2 h (4 °C min–1) in Ar. The CoSA-CN samples were rinsed with ultrapure water and dried overnight at 60 °C.

Fabrication of CoSA@hCN

A mixture of hCN and Co(C5H7O2)2 was dissolved in a 300 mL solution comprising ethanol and acetone in a 1:1 ratio. The solution was stirred at 400 rpm and heated to 75 °C for 2 days for evaporation. The resulting solid was washed with ultrapure water several times and dried in a pre-heated oven at 60 °C overnight. The collected solids were ground and calcined at 550 °C for 2 h (2 °C min–1) in Ar. Finally, the CoSA@hCN solid was collected, rinsed with ultrapure water, and dried overnight at 60 °C.

Electron microscopy

All electron microscopy characterizations were conducted at Adelaide Microscopy, which provides advanced instrumentation for high-resolution structural and compositional analysis at the nanoscale. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging was carried out using an FEI Quanta 450 microscope to examine surface morphology. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observations were performed on an FEI Tecnai G2 Spirit instrument to investigate microstructural features and particle dispersion. High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM), combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) for single-atom metal identification, elemental mapping and compositional analysis, was conducted using an FEI Titan Themis 80−200 microscope.

Physicochemical and surface properties

A specific surface area was acquired by N2 sorption measurement on a Micromeritics Tristar 3000 at −196 °C. The surface potential was analyzed using Zetasizer Nano ZS (Malvern Instruments, Germany). The hydrophilicity property was measured using Attension Optical Tensiometers (Nanoscience Instruments). For each measurement, 30 mg of catalyst powder was pressed into a 7-mm-diameter pellet under a pressure of 1.5 tons to obtain a flat and uniform surface suitable for optical analysis.

Spectroscopy

The Co contents of catalysts were measured by ICP-OES (Agilent 5110) after autoclave digestion of the samples. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed using a Rigaku MiniFlex 600 X-ray diffractometer. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy was carried out on a Nicolet 6700 (Thermo Fisher). Soft X-ray absorption spectra at the C and N K-edges and Co L-edge XANES were measured at the Soft X-ray Spectroscopy beamline of the Australian Synchrotron, part of Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (ANSTO) in Melbourne. Data analysis was performed using the QANT software package provided by the facility.63 Co K-edge XANES and EXAFS spectra were collected in transmission mode at the same synchrotron. Measurements were conducted under ambient conditions. All spectra data were processed using ATHENA mode of the IFEFFIT package for energy calibration, background correction and normalization.64 Surface chemistry of samples was analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) using an X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (K-alpha, Thermo Fisher Scientific). All the binding energies were referenced to the C 1s peak at 284.8 eV. The VB-XPS and UPS spectra were obtained using a Thermo Fisher Scientific ESCALAB Xi spectrometer.

Electronic structure and functions study

UV-visible diffuse reflectance spectra were acquired using a Cary 100 UV-Vis spectrophotometer (Agilent, USA). The band gap was estimated by Tauc plots derived from the Kubelka-Munk function. The position of the valence band was determined through valence band XPS using an X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (K-alpha, Thermo Fisher Scientific, UK). The steady-state photoluminescence (PL) was obtained using an RF-5301PC spectrofluorophotometer (Shimadzu, Japan). The steady-state PL map (variable excitation and emission wavelengths) and TRPL spectra (excitation of 350 nm, emission of 470 nm) were obtained using an FLS1000 spectrometer (Edinburgh Instrument). A Bruker Magnettech ESR5000 was used to measure the Electron Spin Resonance (EPR) signal of solid samples.

Electrochemical measurements

Electrochemical measurements were carried out using a CHI760E electrochemical workstation (standard three-electrode configuration). Open-circuit potential (OCP) measurements were performed in artificial seawater (pH = 8.33) as the electrolyte. A saturated calomel electrode (SCE) served as the reference electrode, and a Pt wire was used as the counter electrode.

The measured potentials can be converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale via the following equation:
ERHE = ESCE + E0SCE + 0.0592 × pH.
Where, ERHE is the converted potential versus RHE, E0SCE is 0.242 V at 25 °C, and ESCE is the experimentally measured potential against SCE reference. The working electrode was prepared by depositing the catalyst onto fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO, 1 × 1.5 cm2) glass. For electrode preparation, 5 mg of catalyst was dispersed in 200 μL isopropanol with 5 μL Nafion solution to form a homogeneous ink. The ink was drop-casted onto a defined circular area (diameter = 5 mm) of the FTO substrate and dried under ambient conditions. Polarization curves were measured using the same three-electrode configuration and electrode preparation method. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted using a similar setup; however, 0.5 M Na2SO4 (pH = 7) was used as the electrolyte. EIS spectra were recorded at open-circuit potential over a frequency range of 105 to 0.01 Hz with an AC amplitude of 0.005 V. All measurements were conducted without iR compensation. The electrochemical analysis was primarily intended for qualitative comparison of interfacial charge-transfer behavior, and the reported potentials are therefore discussed in a comparative rather than absolute benchmarking context. The electrochemical measurements complement the photocatalytic evaluation and are not intended to represent standalone electrocatalytic performance. The photocurrent density measurement was conducted using a similar setup using 0.5 M Na2SO4 (pH = 7) as the electrolyte. A 300 W xenon-arc lamp (Aulight CEL-HX, Beijing, with 420 cut-off filter) was used as a light source.

Photocatalytic H2 production from seawater

The photocatalytic H2 production tests were carried out using a homemade sealed black poly(tetrafluoroethylene) reactor equipped with a quartz window and a water-cooling jacket (Supplementary Fig. 65). A 300 W xenon-arc lamp was used as a light source (emitted UV and visible light, Aulight CEL-HX, Beijing). Visible light-driven photocatalytic H2 production tests were performed using a 420 cut-off filter. The light intensity was measured by a 340 solar meter (OAI, USA), and determined as 147 mW cm–2 at the light spot. A water circulation system was supplied to keep the temperature at 25 °C for the H2 production tests unless further specified. A solution of 0.4 g L–1 photocatalyst and 10 vol% TEOA (as a sacrificial agent) was prepared. Before irradiation, a 1 mg L–1 H2PtCl6 solution was added and vigorously stirred in the dark for 30 min. Ultrapure nitrogen (N2, 99.9%) gas was purged into the system simultaneously, ensuring anaerobic conditions. The H2 product was analyzed using an online gas chromatograph (Agilent 490 Micro GC) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). For, apparent quantum efficiency (AQE) test, the experiment was conducted for 1h under a 300 W xenon-arc lamp using a 420 nm bandpass filter. After adding H2PtCl6 (1 mg L–1) into a pre-mixed suspension of 0.4 g L–1 photocatalyst and 10 vol% TEOA, the mixture was vigorously stirred in the dark for 30 min, followed by irradiation for 30 min photodeposit Pt co-catalysts.

Preparation of the sponge-photoreactor

The illustration of the sponge-photoreactor preparation process is shown in Supplementary Fig. 38. A commercial sponge (Big Job Magic Eraser, Chux) was thoroughly cleaned before catalyst immobilization. The sponge was first immersed in 750 mL of ultrapure water until fully saturated, and then manually compressed to expel the trapped liquid. This process was repeated 10 times until the disappearance of foam in the expelled water to remove residual surfactants. The sponge was then subjected to ultrasonication in 750 mL of 10 vol% ethanol solution for 30 min, followed by three additional cycles of immersion and compression to eliminate any remaining contaminants. The cleaned sponge was dried overnight in a preheated oven at 80 °C and cooled to room temperature for further use. The catalyst slurry was prepared via the following process. Photocatalyst (40 mg) was dispersed in 20 mL of ethanol under magnetic stirring for 30 min. Pt cocatalysts (1.0 wt%, using H2PtCl6 as the precursor) were introduced via photodeposition under light irradiation for 15 min. After Pt loading, 4 mL of TEOA was added and stirred for an additional 15 min. TEOA serves as a mild stabilizing agent and a binding facilitator, promoting both the dispersion of the catalyst and its adhesion to the sponge support. The resulting slurry was transferred to a flat container. The dried sponge was placed with the white side down into the slurry and allowed to absorb the suspension for 15 s. It was then dried in an oven at 60 °C for 1 h. This dip-coating and drying process was repeated twice, and then dried in an oven at 60 °C. Upon cooling to room temperature, the sponge-photoreactor was obtained. Then, the photocatalyst-coated layer was edge-sealed with a ring of standard transparent tape to secure the catalyst layer and reduce lateral wicking. The as-prepared sponge-photoreactor can then be directly employed in seawater for solar H2 production and seawater evaporation.

Integrated photocatalytic H2 production and seawater desalination

A custom-built device was designed to simultaneously enable photocatalytic H2 evolution and solar-driven seawater desalination (Supplementary Fig. 47). The device consists of two compartments, a seawater pool and a purified water collection chamber. The upper enclosure was sealed with a slanted quartz glass window, which allowed efficient light transmission while promoting the condensation of water vapor. The tilted design facilitated a directional flow of condensed droplets into the purified water collection chamber. During operation, the sponge-photoreactor was placed in the seawater pool with the white-coated surface facing upward. Then, 500 mL of seawater was added to the seawater pool. The internal environment was maintained under ambient air conditions to simulate real-world operation. The device was sealed to enable gas accumulation. A 300 W xenon-arc lamp equipped with an AM 1.5 filter was used as a simulated solar light source. The average light intensity was measured by 340 solar meter (OAI, USA) at 5 representative points, and determined as 103 mW cm–2. Gas products were analyzed using a gas chromatograph (GC, Agilent 8890) with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). The purified water was collected from the purified water chamber and quantified gravimetrically. Its metal ion content was determined via atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) to assess desalination performance.

Theoretical calculations

The periodic electronic structure calculations were carried out within the framework of spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP).65,66 The electron-ion interactions were described by the projector augmented wave (PAW) approach.67 The exchange-correlation functional was described within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) formulation. Dispersion interactions of the van der Waals type were described using Grimme’s DFT-D3 semi-empirical correction.68 The plane-wave expansion was truncated at a kinetic energy cutoff of 500 eV. Geometry optimizations were conducted with a Gamma (Γ)-centered 1 × 1 × 1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point grid for Brillouin zone sampling. For surface slab models, a vacuum region of approximately 15 Å was introduced perpendicular to the slab plane to avoid spurious interactions between periodically repeated images. All atomic positions were fully optimized during the relaxation process without any geometric constraint, ensuring unbiased structural evolution toward the minimum-energy configuration. All structures exhibiting magnetic moments were fully relaxed without imposing any constraint. Structural optimization proceeded until the total energy converged to below 1 × 1 × 10-6 eV and the residual forces on each atom were reduced to less than 0.02 eV Å-1. The charge density difference (CDD) was calculated to visualize the redistribution of electronic charge upon the formation of the Co−N coordination environment. The CDD is defined as:
Δρ(r) = ρCoSA + CN (r) − ρCoSA(r) − ρCN(r).
Where, ρCoSA+CN denotes the charge density of the complete Co single-atom structure, and ρCoSA and ρCN represent the charge densities of the isolated Co center and the surrounding N coordination environment, respectively, each computed in the same geometric configuration as in the combined system. This definition highlights the intrinsic charge redistribution between the metal center and its coordinated ligands. The isosurface was visualized at an isovalue of 0.001 e Bohr−3, which provides a clear yet physically meaningful depiction of charge transfer regions. In the plotted isosurfaces, yellow regions denote electron accumulation (Δρ > 0), while cyan regions correspond to electron depletion (Δρ < 0). Thus, the color contrast intuitively reflects the direction and spatial extent of charge transfer between the CN adsorbate and the Co active site.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This study presents a combination of atomic-scale catalyst design and system-level integration for photocatalytic H₂ evolution from seawater. The novelty lies in engineering asymmetric Co–N₄ single-atom sites on carbon nitride with second-shell carbon vacancies to modulate electronic asymmetry and salinity-mediated charge transfer. This work contributed to addressing two long-standing hurdles simultaneously: realizing high catalytic activity in saline environments and coupling hydrogen production with concurrent freshwater generation. The deployment on a scalable floating photothermal platform under sunlight elevates the work from materials discovery to a technology concept with practical relevance, suggesting pathways for modular, off-grid hydrogen supply in coastal or remote settings. To better support the claims and conclusions and improve the quality of this work, the following questions are suggested to be addressed before considering it for publication.
1. Page 3, lines 87-88, Supplementary Fig. 6: TGA is not accurate enough to identify the Co loadings. As shown in the TGA curve, the adsorbed water may contribute to the mass loss during the heating process. To improve this data, ICP-AES/AAS is suggested to measure the Co loadings.
2. It was claimed that carbon vacancies were formed in CoSA-hCN. Elemental analysis is necessary to identify the composition of all three catalysts: CoSA-CN, CoSA@hCN, and CoSA-hCN, especially the C/N ratio in these samples.
3. What is a possible mechanism of forming Co-N4 with carbon vacancies via the silica-templated one-step process?
4. Page 8, line 199-200, Supplementary Fig. 19: VB-XPS alone gives relative VBM to Femi level (EF). A work function from UPS/secondary-electron cutoff or Kelvin probe is required to place the bands on an absolute (vacuum) scale and convert them to SHE/NHE.
5. Page 7, Fig. 2g, lines 223-226: the intensities of Pt peaks from different catalysts vary significantly. What is the exact loading amount of Pt on each catalyst? What is the particle size of Pt on these catalysts? As the Pt nanoparticles act as active sites for the H2 evolution reaction, the particle size and loading amount of Pt nanoparticles on photocatalysts play an important role in the H2 evolution rate. ICP-AES/AAS and HRTEM are required to answer these questions.
6. Page 9, lines 223-228: “It was claimed that the coexistence of Pt0 and Pt2+ species implies a dual functional role…….” Is it possible that the Pt0 in photo-deposited Pt nanoparticles is partially oxidized to Pt2+ when the sample is exposed to air?
7. Page 9, lines 230-232; “Post-deposition Co K-edge XANES spectra reveal a light shift in the absorption edge of CoSA-hCN toward lower energy, indicating partial reduction of Co centers by photoexcited electrons (Fig. 2h).” Is this phenomenon observed on CoSA-hCN only? How about other catalysts after Pt deposition?
8. Material synthesis procedure: What is the pH value of 4 mol/L NH4HF2? Is it a strong acid (pH <1) that can etch the Co species from CoSA-hCN?
9. The catalysts CoSA-CN, CoSA@hCN, and CoSA-hCN with different Co coordination were synthesized via method engineering. which showed remarkably different photocatalytic H2 evolution activity. Material characterizations demonstrated that multiple structural features and properties of these materials were distinct, including surface area, surface hydrophilicity, zeta potential, conductivity, charge transfer, Pt loading (maybe amount and particle size), and band alignment (bandgap and band position). What is the key/major factor contributing to the enhanced H2 evolution rate of CoSA-hCN in pure water and seawater, respectively? For instance, the surface area of CoSA-hCN is three times that of CoSA-CN, and the H2 evolution rate of CoSA-hCN is around 4-fold higher than that of CoSA-CN. Is there a direct relationship between the surface area and the H2 evolution rate?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This work presents a floating photothermal platform designed for the simultaneous production of hydrogen and freshwater from seawater. The approach is innovative, leveraging single-atom cobalt configurations on carbon nitride photocatalysts applied onto foam supports. The rational design of the catalyst, supported by detailed characterizations, clearly demonstrates the originality and significance of the work. The manuscript is well written, and the conclusions are appropriately supported by the presented data.
However, several important aspects related to the practical implementation and long-term stability of the platform need further clarification and discussion:
1. Stability of the active layer: The long-term stability of the photothermal layer on the melamine foam raises concerns, especially under prolonged operation in real seawater environments. The possibility of catalyst leaching and the downward migration of active materials should be more thoroughly investigated. The authors are encouraged to provide quantitative data or estimates on material loss over time, if available.
2. Interaction Between Catalyst and Support: It remains unclear whether there is any chemical or physical interaction between the melamine foam and the catalyst layer. A discussion on this point, supported by surface characterization or adhesion tests, would strengthen the understanding of the structural integrity of the composite system.
3. Gravity-Assisted Re-Accumulation Strategy: The authors mention a gravity-assisted re-accumulation mechanism to mitigate catalyst loss. However, the practical feasibility of this approach under real operational conditions is questionable. Further elaboration is required to assess how effective and scalable this strategy would be in a realistic application scenario, especially in open water environments.
4. Salt Fouling and Long-Term Operation: Salt accumulation or fouling is a major concern for any system operating with seawater. The manuscript should include a discussion on how the platform design addresses this issue, especially regarding the impact of salt crystallization on both photothermal performance and catalyst activity over extended use.
Overall, the study is highly promising and contributes meaningfully to the field. Addressing the points above would greatly improve the manuscript and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the system's robustness and scalability for real-world applications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript presents an interesting study on molecularly engineered single-atom Co catalysts integrated into a scalable photothermal reactor for seawater splitting and desalination. The authors provide a well-designed system with comprehensive structural characterizations, mechanistic analyses, and impressive device-level demonstrations, highlighting strong H evolution activity and freshwater production directly from natural seawater. The integration of photothermal enhancement with catalyst design is an important strength.
However, the central claim of single-atom catalysis requires more careful justification. The experimental results suggest that the primary photocatalytic activity is largely derived from the in situ photodeposited Pt clusters, while the role of the Co single atoms and the hCN substrate remains less clearly distinguished. Theoretical analysis should be clarified to separate the contributions of Pt clusters, Co single atoms, and the carbon nitride support. Furthermore, some mechanistic interpretations (e.g., band center analysis, charge density differences, and spin localization) require stronger evidence and clearer presentation.
Overall, while the work is promising and suitable for publication, I recommend major revision before acceptance. Addressing the mechanistic role of individual components, clarifying computational and experimental analyses, and improving figure annotations will significantly enhance the rigor and impact of this manuscript.
1. Typo: There is a missing closing parenthesis starting with “(characteristic” in Line 112, Page 5:
“The declining i1:i2 ratio (characteristic C atoms in N=C–N2 to N=C–N(NHx) from CoSA-CN to CoSA-hCN and ~”
2. Please provide the isovalue of the charge density difference in Fig. 2, and reduce the isovalue to clearly identify the atomic sites of charge accumulation and depletion. Indicate in the caption:
(a) what the colors in the isosurfaces represent, and
(b) how the charge density difference was calculated (e.g., the difference between CoSA and CN).
3. Since DFT often gives poor predictions of spin localization due to spin-delocalization error, please provide the spin density of CoSA-hCN to justify the asymmetric spin density of states shown in Fig. 2b, as well as to offer insights into its relationship with photocatalytic activity.
4. For all theoretical calculations of adsorption energies (Fig. 3h and i) and the free energy diagram (Supplementary Fig. 30), please specify the active center or adsorption site, or include the optimized structures, to clearly indicate the adsorption configurations.
5. The band center analysis in Supplementary Fig. 34 does not show a clear correlation with the adsorption strength of the Volmer intermediate (*H, Supplementary Fig. 30) or saline ions (Fig. 3h). According to the band center theory, the upshift or downshift of the metal valence (d-)band center near the Fermi level should affect the adsorption strength of intermediates. However, the provided d-band center, if it corresponds to the active metal center, does not correlate with H adsorption energy, while the p- and s-band centers are too far below the Fermi level to modulate the occupation of bonding and antibonding states.
Furthermore, the band center analysis in Supplementary Fig. 34 should specify which element or species it refers to, and it is meaningful only if the band center of the active site (e.g., the Pt cluster) is considered. Since Supplementary Fig. 34 shows an undefined band center, the following statements appear contradictory:
* (below the caption of Supplemetary Fig. 34)
"Among all models, CoSA-hCN displays the moderate band center positions, which is the most favorable alignment to support effective adsorption and dissociation of reactant species"
* (In the Structure-property correlation section)
"In CoSA-hCN, the total and projected Co d-orbital DOSs shift closer to the Fermi level, indicating stronger Co-N orbital interaction and greater charge transfer capability."
In addition, I recommend analyzing the Bader charge of the Pt cluster, since:
(a) it is more meaningful for an isolated cluster than its band center, and
(b) the authors have already mentioned efficient charge transfer in CoSA-hCN.
6. In Fig. 3h and 3i, how did you define the adsorption energy of "charged" ions? Also, to avoid confusion, the y-axis in Fig. 3h should be Eads (eV) with signs consistent with Fig. 3i, rather than using the magnitude of adsorption energy.
7. In the last sentences of "Structure-property correlation" section, the authors suggest a possible mechanism of photoelectron transfer, visualized in Fig. 2i and 5e. Please include the supporting density of states of Pt-cluster-hybridized CoSA-hCN to show the relative positions of projected DOS states of Pt, Co and CN.
8. On Page 9, the authors report post-deposition Co K-edge XANES and state that the lower energy observed in CoSA-hCN indicates "partial reduction of Co centers by photoexcited electrons". Is it sufficient to claim localization of photoexcited electrons at Co centers, considering their limited lifetime?
9. In the computational details, what does "The bottom layers of about half of the structure" mean? Isn't it a single layer structure of hCN? Moreover, the use of “about” is ambiguous and should be clarified.
10. The caption of Supplementary Fig. 19 can be misleading, as it does not show the (theoretical) electronic band structure but the experimentally estimated band edge alignments.
11. Although Co plays a crucial role in relaying photoexcited electrons, the main HER catalytic activity is attributed to the Pt cluster on CoSA-hCN. In this case, how can we describe it as a "single-atom Co photocatalyst"?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
In this work, the authors reported a carbon nitride–supported single-atom cobalt photocatalyst integrated into a floating photothermal device for simultaneous seawater splitting and desalination. The study presents extensive structural characterizations (including XAS and DFT) to support the claim that asymmetric Co–N₄ configurations with second-shell carbon vacancies enhance charge transfer and salinity tolerance. The device-level demonstration of hydrogen and freshwater co-production is ambitious, and the characterization of ion rejection mechanisms is a strength of the work.
However, there are several concerns that limit the impact and clarity of this manuscript. Overall, while the manuscript demonstrates well-characterized materials and an integrated device concept, the mechanistic ambiguity, overstatement of “real-world” relevance, and insufficient benchmarking significantly weaken the impact. These issues should be thoroughly addressed before the manuscript can be considered for publication in Nature Communication.
Major Concerns
1. Although the structural analysis of the catalysts is comprehensive, the manuscript lacks a clear mechanistic link between the observed atomic/electronic modifications and the improvements in hydrogen evolution and photothermal effects. The authors should clarify which structural factors are most important, and how this “molecular engineering single approach” provides a general strategy for improving performance.
2. The reported heating of the CN-based material to ~65 °C (line 294) is unusual given that CN is not black. In the Methods section (line 515), the reactor is described as being constructed from black PTFE. It remains unclear whether the heating originates from the photothermal effect of the CoSA–CA catalyst itself or from the reactor substrate. This ambiguity raises concerns about the interpretation of photothermal contributions.
3. The role of photothermal effects is not adequately explained. The authors should provide a mechanistic discussion of how the CoSA–CA structure contributes to photothermal enhancement and how this property translates into improved desalination and HER performance.
4. The system relies on triethanolamine (TEOA) as a sacrificial electron donor. This is not sustainable and contradicts the claim that the device has been tested under “real-world” conditions. The authors should moderate their claims, as the use of TEOA fundamentally differentiates the system from practical overall water splitting.
5. When comparing results with the literature, the authors do not distinguish between sacrificial hydrogen production and overall water-splitting systems. Since sacrificial systems typically exhibit higher HER rates, the current comparisons risk overstating the relative performance of the reported catalyst (Fig.5).
In addition, a few minor points should be addressed:
1. It is unclear how the contact angle measurements in Fig. 3 were conducted (directly on powders, or on films drop-cast onto substrates). This should be clarified.
2. In Supplementary Tables S6 and S7, systems using sacrificial agents should be clearly separated from overall water-splitting systems.
3. The justification for designing the system specifically for seawater use requires more careful discussion. In practice, desalination contributes less than 5% of the overall energy cost of green hydrogen production, and the broader benefits of seawater utilization should be explained.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
This manuscript reports on molecular engineering of single atom catalysts in a scalable photothermal reactor for integrated seawater splitting and desalination. The authors constructed three single-atom Co configurations on CN: symmetric Co–N4 (CoSA-CN), vacancy-anchored Co–N3 (CoSA@hCN), and asymmetric Co–N4 with second-shell carbon vacancies (CoSA-hCN). The asymmetric Co–N4 in hierarchically porous carbon nitride (CoSA-hCN) introduces second-shell carbon vacancies that reshape electronic asymmetry and charge dynamics, establishing a robust pathway for effective salinity-mediated charge transfer and in situ Pt photodeposition for H2 evolution. On a scalable 60 cm2 floating photothermal platform with one sun, simultaneous H2 (47.7 mmol m−2 h−1) and freshwater (1.88 kg m−2 h−1) are produced directly from natural seawater. Given the significance of this work in advancing a generalizable design paradigm for integrated solar hydrogen production and seawater desalination, it merits publication in Nature Communications, a leading multidisciplinary journal, provided that the following comments are addressed thoroughly.
1. What is the reason for choosing CoSA-hCN as the catalyst? I believe the main novelty of this work lies in the integration of a photothermal reactor for seawater splitting and desalination (ref. 20 in the manuscript), along with floatable systems for photocatalysis (ref. 33 in the Supplementary Information), which synergistically enhance both solar hydrogen production and seawater desalination. The novelty does not primarily reside in the catalyst design itself. Honestly, I believe the choice of photocatalyst is less important in this case than the integration of the two systems. Could the author expand the reactions with other photocatalysts (TiO2, ZnO, CdS….) with proper cocatalyst deposition, and compare the result with CoSA-hCN, to justify their choice of photocatalyst?
2. While photothermal systems are properly referenced (refs. 20–25), floatable photocatalyst systems are rarely cited in the manuscript. The authors should properly reference recent developments in floatable photocatalyst systems and compare their merits with the state-of-the-art in the main manuscript.
3. While the authors demonstrated that their system operates stably for 6 * 6-hour cycles, they did not provide in-depth characterization of the spent catalyst. Although they claim that the asymmetric Co–N₄ sites in CoSA-hCN introduce second-shell carbon vacancies that reshape electronic asymmetry and charge dynamics—establishing a robust pathway for effective salinity-mediated charge transfer—it remains questionable whether the initial active site structure is preserved during operation.

Comment 4-8: The justification for designing the system specifically for seawater use requires more
careful discussion. In practice, desalination contributes less than 5% of the overall energy cost of green
hydrogen production, and the broader benefits of seawater utilization should be explained.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that the direct energy cost of
desalination contributes only a minor portion of the overall green hydrogen production process. Our
intention is not to position seawater utilization as an energy-saving strategy. The motivation for designing
a seawater-compatible system lies in the broader practical, environmental, and infrastructural benefits
that extend beyond the energy balance. Specifically, a direct use of seawater enables access to an
abundant, non-competitive water source, which is particularly important for arid, water-scarce, or rapidly
industrializing coastal regions. Moreover, seawater-compatible systems have the potential to reduce the
environmental footprint associated with large centralized desalination infrastructure, including brine
discharge and land use. We have clarified these points in the revised manuscript to more accurately reflect
the practical and environmental motivation for seawater-compatible devices.
